concept.name: Consistent Hashing
concept.tagline: Distributing data dynamically across heterogeneous clusters without central coordination.

spark.summary: In distributed caching and storage, traditional modulo routing `hash(key) % N` remaps nearly 100% of keys whenever a server crashes or joins, triggering catastrophic cache stampedes. Consistent Hashing maps both data keys and server nodes onto the same virtual 32-bit ring ($0$ to $2^{32}-1$). Adding or removing a node only migrates $1/N$ of the keys, bounding rebalancing overhead and shielding database origins.
spark.keyTakeaway: Traditional modulo hashing destroys cache hit ratios during cluster resizing. Consistent hashing bounds key reassignment to $K/N$, while Virtual Nodes (vNodes) ensure mathematically balanced load distribution across physical hardware.

concept.whyItMatters: Dynamic scaling in distributed storage (e.g. DynamoDB, Cassandra, Memcached clusters) requires elastic addition and removal of nodes without downtime. Without consistent hashing, single-node churn cascades into cluster-wide cache invalidation and database collapse.
keyPoints: Maps data keys and server addresses onto a shared 32-bit integer space (the Hash Ring: 0 to 2^32 - 1).
Keys are assigned to the first server encountered when traversing the ring clockwise.
When a node joins or fails, only the keys between that node and its predecessor are reassigned (falling forward to the next clockwise node). Disruption is bounded to 1/N.
Virtual Nodes (vNodes) solve hash clustering: each physical node hashes multiple times (e.g. ServerA#1, ServerA#2), interleaving servers across the ring for uniform distribution.
whenToUse: Distributed in-memory caching clusters (Memcached, Redis clusters) where cache miss storms must be avoided during scale-out/scale-in.
Distributed NoSQL storage systems (Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB, Riak) requiring partitioned, decentralized data ownership.
Load balancers routing persistent user sessions or WebSockets to backend worker fleets.
whenNotToUse: Single-server architectures or small fixed clusters with zero node churn.
Relational databases relying on global ACID transactions across multiple foreign keys.

examples.title: Elastic Cache Resizing Under Traffic Surge
examples.scenario: A black-friday e-commerce cluster scales its Redis nodes from 10 to 12. Modulo hashing would have evicted 83% of keys. Consistent hashing migrates only 16.6% (1/6th) of keys.
examples.outcome: Cache hit ratio stays above 94%, origin database CPU stays below 35%, and zero outages occur.

tradeOffs.pro: Adding 100–256 vNodes per physical server reduces load imbalance variance to under 5%.
tradeOffs.con: Routing lookup table requires $O(V cdot N)$ memory and $O(\log(V \cdot N))$ binary search overhead per request.

failureModes.name: Cascading Hotspot Collapse without vNodes
failureModes.description: If physical nodes hash unevenly, a crashed node dumps 100% of its load onto its single clockwise neighbor, causing it to crash and triggering a domino collapse.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce a minimum of 128 virtual nodes per physical host with proactive replication across successor nodes.

commonMistakes: Using a weak 32-bit hash function (like naive MD5 or Java hashCode) causing hash clustering instead of cryptographic Murmur3 or xxHash.
Failing to replicate keys across $R$ successive distinct physical nodes (instead of successive vNodes).
